fields.title: Estimate consequences before doing
fields.keyTakeaway: A simple four-factor model answers the "is it worth doing at all" question in half an hour. Its value is not in forecast accuracy, but in showing which factor actually matters.
fields.checkQuestion: An improvement will raise the step's conversion from 20% to 24%. How do you tell if that is a lot or a little?
fields.blocks/0/text: The key question of the node: **what will happen if the metrics change?** Ask it before starting the work, not after.
fields.blocks/1/text: **What happens if you do not answer this question.** The team takes on an improvement that yields three percent where it affects nothing, and skips one where the same percent costs ten times more.
fields.blocks/2/subtitle: A chain of factors and one question for each
fields.blocks/2/items/0: **1. Write down the metric as a product** — result = A × B × C × D.
fields.blocks/2/items/2: **3. Change them one at a time** by a realistic amount and observe the result.
fields.blocks/2/items/3: **4. Find the sensitive factor** — the one where a small change yields a large effect. Usually there is only one.
fields.blocks/3/text:
Paying users = visits × registration × activation × payment.
Now: 40 000 × 8% × 41% × 37% = 485.

What an improvement by a quarter gives:
registration 8% → 10%: +121 paying
activation 41% → 51%: +118
payment 37% → 46%: +118

All three are roughly equal — meaning you should choose by cost, not by effect. Doubling visits gives +485, but costs a budget that is not there.

Half an hour of work resolved the debate over what matters more.
fields.blocks/4/text: If the factors are not independent — for instance, traffic growth degrades conversion — simple multiplication lies. You can tell by looking: check whether the factors moved together in the past.
fields.blocks/4/title: The model calculates what you put into it
fields.blocks/5/text: This is an order-of-magnitude estimate, not a forecast: a twofold error here is normal and does not prevent you from deciding whether it is worth it. Do not use this model for promises to the business — that requires data, not back-of-the-envelope arithmetic.
